```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(crywolf)
# print one block of the Stan program, read from the installed file so that
# the excerpts never drift from the code that runs
stan_lines <- readLines(fp_stan_file())
stan_block <- function(name) {
  start <- grep(paste0("^", name, " \\{"), stan_lines)
  end <- start + which(stan_lines[(start + 1):length(stan_lines)] == "}")[1]
  cat(stan_lines[start:end], sep = "\n")
}
```

`fp_occu()` fits one Stan program for every model in the package: the
multiple-methods design of Miller et al. (2011), its observation-confirmation
variant (Chambert et al., 2015), and the standard occupancy model. This
article walks through it for readers who want to know exactly what is
estimated, or who want to change it. The model itself is described in
`vignette("crywolf", package = "crywolf")`; here the focus is on how it is
coded. The program is a file installed with the package:

```{r path, eval = FALSE}
fp_stan_file()
```

`fp_compile()` copies it to the user cache directory and compiles it the
first time it is needed, so later sessions reuse the executable.

## Data

`fp_occu()` turns the `fp_data` object and the formulas into the list that
Stan reads, which is kept in the fitted object as `m$stan_data`. The data
block declares it:

```{r data-block, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
stan_block("data")
```

The occupancy design `X`, the detection design `Z`, and the false-positive
design `Xfp` are model matrices built from the formulas. `Xfp` has no
intercept column, because the intercept of the false-positive rate is not a
free parameter (see below). Switches turn parts of the model on and off:
`estimate_fp = 0` gives the standard occupancy model (`fp = NULL`),
`Kfp = 0` the constant false-positive rate, `estimate_re = 1` the recorder
random intercept, and `obs_confirm = 1` the observation-confirmation design.
The prior scales are data too, which is why `fp_priors()` can change them
without recompiling.

### Binomial rows

Automated occasions do not enter one by one. Occasions of the same site
with identical detection covariates (and recorder) are collapsed into one
row with `n2` trials and `y2` detections. Given the occupancy state, the
occasions of a site are independent Bernoulli trials with the same
probability, so the product of their likelihoods equals the binomial
likelihood without its coefficient, which does not depend on the
parameters. The posterior is therefore exactly the same, and the model is
much faster when detection covariates are constant within sites. With
occasion-level covariates, such as the acoustic indices of the
`vignette("curiango", package = "crywolf")` data, each occasion is its own
row. Rows are sorted by site, and `start2` and `len2` give the first row and
the number of rows of each site.

## Parameters

```{r parameters, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
stan_block("parameters")
stan_block("transformed parameters")
```

The recorder effects are written as `sigma_u * u_raw`, with `u_raw`
standard normal (the non-centred parametrization), which samples better
when there are few recorders or little information about their variance.

With `random_fp = TRUE` (`estimate_fp_re = 1`), the site effects on the
false-positive rate are written in the same way, `sigma_fp[1] * e_raw`, and
are added to its linear predictor; with the option off, `e_raw` and
`sigma_fp` have length zero and the model is the same as without them.

The false-positive intercept is not a parameter of its own:
`gamma0 = alpha[1] - fp_gap`, with `fp_gap` constrained to be positive.
Because column 1 of `Z` is the intercept, `alpha[1]` is the logit of true
detection at the reference values of the covariates (all zero), and the gap
keeps the false-positive rate below it there. Without this constraint, the
likelihood has a second mode in which occupied and unoccupied sites swap
roles, and the sampler could visit either.

## Likelihood

The occupancy state $z_i$ is discrete, so Stan cannot sample it. The
function `site_loglik()` sums it out for each site in a range of sites, from
`a` to `b`:

```{r functions, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
stan_block("functions")
```

For site $i$, `occ[i]` accumulates the log-likelihood of all its data if
the site is occupied and `unocc[i]` if it is not; the site's contribution
is then

$$
\log\left[\psi_i \exp(\text{occ}_i) + (1 - \psi_i) \exp(\text{unocc}_i)\right],
$$

computed with `log_sum_exp()` for numerical stability. Three cases
shortcut it:

- A site with a verified detection (`known_present`) must be occupied, so
  only the first term is kept.
- Under the standard model (`estimate_fp = 0`), an automated detection also
  proves occupancy, so `unocc[i]` is set to $-\infty$.
- Under the observation-confirmation design, an occasion confirmed to hold
  a true observation ($v_3 \geq 2$) rules out the unoccupied state in the
  same way.

The per-occasion terms are computed as vectors and summed by site with
`segment()`, which works because the rows of each site are contiguous. For
the automated occasions the binomial log-likelihood is written as
$y \eta - n \log(1 + e^{\eta})$, where $\eta$ is the linear predictor;
this equals $y \log p + (n - y) \log(1 - p)$ with $p$ the inverse logit of
$\eta$, but needs one transcendental function per row instead of two. The
verified occasions enter as the number of occasions and detections of each
site, which gives the same sum as one Bernoulli term per occasion.

### Parallel likelihood

Most of the computing time goes to the automated occasions: in the
`vignette("curiango", package = "crywolf")` data, with 97,806 one-minute
occasions and a recorder effect, they took about 90% of the time spent
evaluating the log density. Because sites are independent given the
parameters, the model block adds them up with `reduce_sum()`, which splits
the sites into slices and evaluates the slices on different threads.
`partial_loglik()` is the sum of `site_loglik()` over one slice; each slice
reads only its own rows of the automated and confirmed occasions, located
with `start2` and `len2` (and their counterparts for the confirmed
occasions, built in `transformed data`).

`fp_compile()` builds the model with threading enabled, and
`fp_occu(threads_per_chain = )` sets the number of threads of each chain.
With one thread the sum is computed serially, as before. With more, only
the order of the additions changes, so the log density differs from the
serial one by floating-point rounding (around $10^{-16}$ in relative
terms). Chains with the same seed then follow the same path for a while
and drift apart later, as they would on another computer, and the
posterior is the same. The gain is largest when there are many occasions:
keep `parallel_chains * threads_per_chain` at or below the number of
physical cores.

## Priors and model block

```{r model, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
stan_block("model")
```

All priors are on the logit scale and are listed with their defaults in
`?fp_priors`. The model block adds the sum over sites, computed by
`reduce_sum()`, to the log density.

## Generated quantities

```{r gq, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
stan_block("generated quantities")
```

`log_lik` holds one value per site, with $z_i$ summed out, so `loo()` on a
fitted model gives leave-one-site-out cross-validation: a site with all its
occasions is the unit left out. `p11_ref` and `p10_ref` are the true- and
false-detection probabilities at the reference values of the covariates,
`p10_bar` is the false-positive rate averaged over the sites in the data,
and `r11` is the detection probability of the verified method
(`p_verified` in the output of `fp_occu()`).

## Modifying a copy

To change the model, for example its priors' families or the structure of
a submodel, edit a copy of the file and fit it with 'cmdstanr' directly,
using the data list that `fp_occu()` prepared:

```{r modify, eval = FALSE}
file.copy(fp_stan_file(), "my_fp_occu.stan")
# ... edit my_fp_occu.stan ...
sim <- simulate_fp(seed = 1)
m <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE)  # for the data list
my_model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model("my_fp_occu.stan")
my_fit <- my_model$sample(data = m$stan_data, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4,
                          adapt_delta = 0.95)
my_fit$summary(c("beta", "alpha", "fp_gap", "p10_ref"))
```

A copy compiled without `cpp_options = list(stan_threads = TRUE)` runs the
likelihood on one thread per chain, which gives the same results. The
result is a `CmdStanMCMC` object with the Stan names of the
parameters (`beta`, `alpha`, `gamma0`, ...), not an `fp_occu` object, so the
methods of crywolf do not apply to it. If the edit adds data, add the new
elements to the list before sampling. `fp_ppc()` recomputes the likelihood
in R from the posterior draws, so it describes the original model, not an
edited one.

positive detections in species occurrence data under different study
designs. *Ecology*, 96, 332–339. https://doi.org/10.1890/14-1507.1

Miller, D. A., Nichols, J. D., McClintock, B. T., Grant, E. H. C., Bailey,
L. L., & Weir, L. A. (2011). Improving occupancy estimation when two types of
observational error occur: non-detection and species misidentification.
*Ecology*, 92, 1422–1428. https://doi.org/10.1890/10-1396.1
